audit: The connector analogy distinguishes connection from permission, but the existing process diagrams do not let readers inspect a particular advertised capability against a pinned host catalog. Lesson A gives the host, connection and server concrete contents and makes a server-only destructive capability visibly absent from model exposure. Lesson B supplies a request whose schema and identity checks pass while its resource permission fails. Readers must explain why invocation stops despite technical compatibility. Neither lesson adds protocol-version claims or treats annotations as authority. The examples retain separate host and server responsibilities and explicitly distinguish model proposals from MCP messages.

lessons.title: One connection, two different catalogs
lessons.intro: AegisOps connects to the approved observability server. Its model may inspect latency, but the server also advertises a restart capability. Inspect what each container actually owns.

relations: Host chooses which contracts reach its model.
Client connects to server; it grants no authority.

read: Compare the host list with the larger server catalog.
The connection transports requests; it does not choose task permissions.
The server still checks each invocation against its resource policy.
lessons.question: Does advertising restart_service make it callable by the model?
lessons.answer: No. The host has withheld that capability. Server discovery describes availability; exposure requires host review, and any eventual invocation still requires independent authorization.
lessons.takeaway: Discovery describes capabilities; the host chooses exposure.
lessons.assumption: Fictional registry; compatible transport is assumed. Containers show ownership, not an execution sequence.

lessons.title: Valid arguments, forbidden service
lessons.intro: A permitted latency tool receives a structurally valid request for payroll-api. The authenticated caller is allowed to inspect checkout-api only.

checks.label: Resource authority
checks.detail: Only checkout-api is in this grant

read: The requested window satisfies the schema.
An authenticated identity is not a grant for every service.
The resource check rejects this particular target.
lessons.question: Would marking the tool read-only change the decision?
lessons.answer: No. Read-only describes effects, not entitlement to sensitive metrics. The request still targets a service outside this caller's authorized resource scope.
lessons.takeaway: Read-only operations still require resource authorization.
lessons.assumption: Fictional identity and policy; the host permits the tool, but the server restricts resources.
